**Trap:** Students sometimes confuse the tinais with rivers or varnas. The five tinais are geographical-ecological zones, each linked to a distinct landscape and mood in Sangam poetry.

questions.subject: history
questions.question:
Consider the statements:
1. The Sangam poems include Ettutogai (Eight Anthologies) and Pattuppattu (Ten Idylls).
2. Tolkappiyam was composed by Tolkappiyar and is the earliest Tamil grammatical text.
3. Jainism and Buddhism had some influence on Sangam literature but the dominant religion was Shaiva/Vaishnava Bhakti.
Which are correct?
questions.explanation:
All three statements are correct. Ettutogai (Eight Anthologies) and Pattuppattu (Ten Idylls) are the two main Sangam poetic compilations. Tolkappiyam by Tolkappiyar is the earliest Tamil grammar. While Jain and Buddhist ideas appear in some Sangam poems, the dominant religious ethos of the period was Shaiva and Vaishnava bhakti, celebrated in hymns like those of the Nayanars and Alvars.

**Trap:** Statement 3 is sometimes rejected by students who overemphasize the Jain-Buddhist presence; in fact the bhakti strand is the defining religious feature of the late Sangam and post-Sangam.

questions.subject: history
questions.question: The Tripartite Struggle for Kanauj was fought among:
questions.explanation:
The Tripartite Struggle (c. 8th-10th centuries CE) was the long rivalry among the three great powers of the period — the Palas of Bengal, the Pratiharas of western India, and the Rashtrakutas of the Deccan — for control of the holy city of Kanauj and the fertile Gangetic heartland. The Cholas were a contemporary South Indian power but did not participate in this northern contest.

**Trap:** Option D substitutes the Cholas for the Rashtrakutas, and C inserts the Pallavas. The Tripartite Struggle is exclusively a Pala-Pratihara-Rashtrakuta contest.
questions.wikilink: [[../../history/11 - Tripartite Struggle and Cholas.md#Content|Tripartite Struggle and Cholas — source chapter]]

questions.subject: history
questions.question: The founder of the Chola Dynasty (in its later phase) was:
questions.explanation:
Vijayalaya Chola (c. 850-871 CE) captured Thanjavur from the Muttaraiyars and founded the medieval (Imperial) Chola line. Rajaraja I and Rajendra I are later great rulers of the dynasty he founded. Karikala Chola belongs to the much earlier Sangam-era Early Cholas.

**Trap:** Rajaraja I is the dynasty's most famous ruler but is not its founder; Karikala Chola belongs to the Early Cholas of the Sangam period, separated by several centuries.
questions.wikilink: [[../../history/11 - Tripartite Struggle and Cholas.md#Content|Tripartite Struggle and Cholas — source chapter]]

questions.subject: history
questions.question: Rajaraja I built which great temple?
questions.explanation:
The Brihadeeshwara (Rajarajeshwara) Temple at Thanjavur, completed c. 1010 CE, was built by Rajaraja I and is one of the finest examples of Dravidian architecture, with its towering vimana over the sanctum. The Meenakshi Temple at Madurai is associated with the later Nayaka period; the Kailasa Temple at Ellora was excavated by the Rashtrakuta Krishna I; and the Shore Temple at Mahabalipuram is a Pallava monument.

**Trap:** Brihadeeshwara Temple and the Kailasa Temple are both architectural landmarks of the period and are easily confused; their patrons belong to different dynasties.
questions.wikilink: [[../../history/11 - Tripartite Struggle and Cholas.md#Content|Tripartite Struggle and Cholas — source chapter]]

questions.subject: history
questions.question: Rajendra I assumed the title:
questions.explanation:
Rajendra I (c. 1014-1044 CE) took the title Gangaikondachola ("the Chola who conquered the Ganga") after his celebrated northern campaign that reached the Ganga river. To mark this feat he founded a new capital, Gangaikondacholapuram, where he built a second great Brihadeeshwara temple. Uttama Chola was a ruler between Parantaka I and Rajaraja I; Mummadi Chola is a general epithet for a mid-ranking Chola; Vikrama Chola was a later 12th-century ruler.

**Trap:** Uttama Chola and Mummadi Chola are genuine Chola titles/epithets but do not match Rajendra I. The distinctive conquest title of Rajendra I is Gangaikondachola.
questions.wikilink: [[../../history/11 - Tripartite Struggle and Cholas.md#Content|Tripartite Struggle and Cholas — source chapter]]

questions.subject: history
questions.question: A student reads that a Chola monarch invaded the Chalukyan capital of Manyakheta, sacked the Rashtrakuta heartland, and successfully reached the Ganga. The monarch being described is:
questions.explanation:
Rajendra I inherited a strong realm from his father Rajaraja I and extended it dramatically: he campaigned against the Chalukyas, sacked the Rashtrakuta capital Manyakheta (modern Malkhed), and led the celebrated northern expedition that reached the Ganga — earning him the title Gangaikondachola. Parantaka I fought the Rashtrakutas and Pandyas but did not reach the Ganga; Aditya I defeated the Pallavas and consolidated Chola power but stayed in the south.

**Trap:** Rajaraja I is Rajendra I's father and the dynasty's other great conqueror, but the Ganga expedition was Rajendra I's personal achievement.
questions.wikilink: [[../../history/11 - Tripartite Struggle and Cholas.md#Content|Tripartite Struggle and Cholas — source chapter]]

questions.subject: history
questions.question: Which of the following was a significant administrative reform of Rajaraja I?

options.text: Systematic revenue survey and detailed copper-plate records (like the Uttaramerur inscriptions)
Transfer of capital from Tanjore to Madurai

questions.explanation:
Rajaraja I (and his successors) carried out systematic revenue surveys, maintained detailed accounts in copper-plate inscriptions, and regulated village self-government — practices later exemplified in the Uttaramerur inscriptions. The Iqta system was a Turko-Afghan revenue-military institution of the Delhi Sultanate, unrelated to the Cholas. The Cholas maintained, not abandoned, a powerful standing army and navy; and the Chola capital remained at Thanjavur (and later at Gangaikondacholapuram), never at Madurai.

**Trap:** Option D is tempting because Madurai was a major Chola conquest, but it was never the Chola capital.
questions.wikilink: [[../../history/11 - Tripartite Struggle and Cholas.md#Content|Tripartite Struggle and Cholas — source chapter]]

questions.subject: history
questions.question: The Chola practice of "kadamai" referred to:
questions.explanation:
Kadamai was the Chola term for the land revenue (or economic obligation/due) owed by cultivators to the state or temple. Its assessment and remission were major concerns of Chola administration, recorded in detail in copper-plate grants and temple inscriptions. Chola military units were generally termed padai or senais; the ministerial council was not called kadamai; and the term has no musical connotation.

**Trap:** Option A is wrong because military terminology under the Cholas uses padai/senai. Kadamai is specifically an economic-revenue term.
questions.wikilink: [[../../history/11 - Tripartite Struggle and Cholas.md#Content|Tripartite Struggle and Cholas — source chapter]]

questions.subject: history
questions.question:
Match the following rulers with their association:

| Ruler | Association |
|---|---|
| 1. Rajaraja I | a. Built Gangaikondacholapuram |
| 2. Rajendra I | b. Built Brihadeeshwara Temple |
| 3. Karikala Chola | c. Built Kallanai (Grand Anicut) dam |
questions.explanation:
Rajaraja I built the Brihadeeshwara Temple at Thanjavur (1-b). Rajendra I founded Gangaikondacholapuram and built the new Brihadeeshwara temple there to mark his Ganga campaign (2-a). Karikala Chola of the Sangam era is credited with building the Kallanai (Grand Anicut) dam across the Kaveri (3-c). The other options swap or scramble these pairings.

**Trap:** Both Rajaraja I and Rajendra I built Brihadeeshwara temples (at Thanjavur and Gangaikondacholapuram respectively); careful reading of the associations in the table is essential to pick the right pair.
questions.wikilink: [[../../history/11 - Tripartite Struggle and Cholas.md#Content|Tripartite Struggle and Cholas — source chapter]]

questions.subject: history
questions.question: Which of the following is INCORRECT about the Chola administration?

options.text: The kingdom was divided into mandalams (provinces), nadus (districts) and kurrams (villages)
The village assembly was called the ur or mahasabha
The Cholas had a powerful standing army and a navy that projected power overseas
The Chola rulers were primarily feudatories of the Pandyas and never exercised direct rule

questions.explanation:
Statement D is INCORRECT. The Imperial Cholas (especially from Aditya I onwards, and even more powerfully under Rajaraja I and Rajendra I) exercised direct sovereignty over a vast realm; they were not Pandyas' feudatories — in fact, they eclipsed the Pandyas and reduced them to a subordinate role for long stretches. Statements A, B, and C correctly describe Chola administration: the mandalam-nadu-kurram hierarchy, the ur/mahasabha village assemblies, and the formidable Chola army and navy (which raided Srivijaya and the Maldives).

**Trap:** Students familiar with the Sangam Age sometimes wrongly assume all Tamil dynasties had a vague federal relationship. The Imperial Cholas ruled directly from Thanjavur.
questions.wikilink: [[../../history/11 - Tripartite Struggle and Cholas.md#Content|Tripartite Struggle and Cholas — source chapter]]

questions.subject: history
questions.question:
Arrange in chronological order:
1. Founder Vijayalaya Chola
2. Rajaraja I
3. Rajendra I
4. Kulottunga I (Chola-Chalukya)
questions.explanation:
Vijayalaya Chola founded the medieval dynasty (c. 850 CE). His successors led to Parantaka I, then Rajaraja I (r. 985-1014 CE), followed by his son Rajendra I (r. 1014-1044 CE). Several later rulers intervene, and then Kulottunga I — a Chola-Chalukya (son of Rajendra I's daughter and a Chalukya prince) — comes to the throne c. 1070 CE. Hence the correct chronological order is 1 (Vijayalaya) -> 2 (Rajaraja I) -> 3 (Rajendra I) -> 4 (Kulottunga I).

**Trap:** Option B swaps Rajaraja I and Rajendra I. The dynasty's founding comes first, then its two great consecutive conquerors, then Kulottunga I.
questions.wikilink: [[../../history/11 - Tripartite Struggle and Cholas.md#Content|Tripartite Struggle and Cholas — source chapter]]

questions.subject: history
questions.question:
Consider the statements about the Tripartite Struggle:
1. Pratihara ruler Nagabhata II (c. 805-833 CE) is the earliest notable figure who briefly held Kanauj.
2. The Pala ruler Dharmapala also held Kanauj for a time and tried to install his protege Chakrayudha.
3. The conflict ended decisively with the Rashtrakuta Indra III seizing Kanauj around 916 CE.
Which are correct?
questions.explanation:
All three statements are correct. Nagabhata II of the Pratiharas was indeed the first of the three rivals to capture Kanauj (c. early 9th century). Dharmapala of Bengal held Kanauj in turn and installed his protege Chakrayudha on the throne there, an act which triggered Pratihara counter-campaigns. The struggle's decisive late phase saw the Rashtrakuta Indra III capture Kanauj c. 916 CE, after which the Pala and Pratihara positions in the north collapsed.

**Trap:** Statement 1 is sometimes missed because Nagabhata II is less famous than Dharmapala or Indra III, but he is the first to hold Kanauj among the three rivals. The Tripartite Struggle is therefore correctly summarised by all three statements together.
questions.wikilink: [[../../history/11 - Tripartite Struggle and Cholas.md#Content|Tripartite Struggle and Cholas — source chapter]]

questions.subject: history
questions.question: The Chola "Vellan" and "Padai" inscriptions refer to:

options.text: Village-level self-governance and military mobilization records

questions.explanation:
Vellan inscriptions are Chola records concerning the Vellala (cultivator) community and village-level obligations, often detailing local assemblies (ur/mahasabha), land grants and revenue (kadamai) arrangements. Padai inscriptions relate to the padai (military) — orders mobilising troops, supplying equipment, and maintaining military camps. Together they are evidence of Chola administrative-military reach at the village and garrison level. Chola coinage is discussed under different inscription series; the Sangam literary corpus is the Ettutogai/Pattuppattu; and Chola grants to Buddhist viharas were uncommon (the dynasty was largely Shaiva and Vaishnava in patronage).

**Trap:** Option D misreads Chola religious patronage. The Cholas were predominantly temple-builders for Shiva and Vishnu, and padai/vellan inscriptions are administrative, not religious-grant, records.
questions.wikilink: [[../../history/11 - Tripartite Struggle and Cholas.md#Content|Tripartite Struggle and Cholas — source chapter]]

questions.subject: history
questions.question: The First Battle of Tarain (1191) was fought between Prithviraj Chauhan and:
questions.explanation:
The First Battle of Tarain (1191) was fought between the Rajput king Prithviraj Chauhan of Ajmer and the Ghurid invader Muhammad Ghori; Prithviraj won this battle. Muhammad Ghori returned to defeat Prithviraj in the Second Battle of Tarain (1192), which effectively opened the way for Muslim rule in north India. Aibak was Ghori's commander and later founded the Slave Dynasty; Iltutmish was Aibak's successor; Genghis Khan was a Central Asian conqueror with no role at Tarain.

**Trap:** Option B (Aibak) and C (Iltutmish) confuse the general with the dynasty's founder and successor. Genghis Khan is a tempting distractor for any 12th-century Central Asian context but is unrelated.

questions.subject: history
questions.question: Who was the founder of the Slave Dynasty?
questions.explanation:
Qutb-ud-din Aibak (r. 1206-1210 CE), a former slave-general of Muhammad Ghori, became the first Sultan of Delhi and founded the Slave (Mamluk) Dynasty after Ghori's assassination in 1206. He was followed by Aram Shah and then Iltutmish, who made the Sultanate stable and hereditary in his own line. Balban (r. 1266-1287 CE) ended the Slave Dynasty; Alauddin Khalji was a Khalji Dynasty ruler.

**Trap:** Iltutmish is often credited as the dynasty's effective consolidator, but the founder was Aibak. Balban is a late Slave Dynasty ruler, not its founder.

questions.subject: history
questions.question: Qutb-ud-din Aibak was given the title:
questions.explanation:
Qutb-ud-din Aibak earned the title Lakh Baksh ("giver of lakhs") for his reputed generosity on the battlefield of the Second Battle of Tarain (1192), where tradition says he scattered gold from his war-tent. Sipahsalar was a title used by Balban. Tuti-Hind ("parrot of India") was a title associated with Amir Khusrau. Saif-i-Sultani was a title given to Muhammad bin Tughlaq.

**Trap:** Balban's Sipahsalar and Muhammad bin Tughlaq's Saif-i-Sultani are both real Sultanate-era titles, so distractors A and D confuse Aibak with later Sultans.

questions.subject: history
questions.question: The last ruler of the Delhi Sultanate was:
questions.explanation:
Ibrahim Lodi (r. 1517-1526 CE) was the last ruler of the Delhi Sultanate; he was defeated and killed by Babur at the First Battle of Panipat (1526), which marked the end of the Sultanate and the start of Mughal rule. Firoz Shah Tughlaq ruled much earlier (r. 1351-1388 CE); Sikandar Lodi and Bahlul Lodi preceded Ibrahim within the Lodi Dynasty itself.

**Trap:** Firoz Shah Tughlaq is the most famous Tughlaq ruler for reforms, but the Sultanate ended nearly 140 years after him, with Ibrahim Lodi.

questions.subject: history
questions.question: A student reads that a Sultan introduced "market control" regulations, fixed prices, and a network of spies, and his wealth financed a large standing army. The Sultan being described is:
questions.explanation:
Alauddin Khalji (r. 1296-1316 CE) introduced sweeping market-control (hisbah) regulations in Delhi: he fixed the prices of grains, cloth and other essentials, appointed officers (diwan-i-riyasat) and a network of spies to enforce them, and used the resulting revenue surplus to maintain a large standing army at low cost. These price-control and espionage measures are a hallmark of his reign and appear in Amir Khusrau's account. Muhammad bin Tughlaq is famous for ambitious but failed projects (token currency, capital transfer), not market control. Balban centralised royal authority and the espionage system but did not run commodity price-fixing on Alauddin's scale. Firoz Shah Tughlaq was known for welfare measures, not market control.

**Trap:** Distractors include Sultans famous for one big reform each, but the specific combination of price-fixing, spies and army-financing is uniquely Alauddin Khalji's.

questions.subject: history
questions.question: Which of the following is INCORRECT about the Delhi Sultanate?

options.text: Alauddin Khalji was the first Sultan to issue "Sikka" (coinage)
Muhammad bin Tughlaq's token currency was withdrawn after public protest
Firoz Shah Tughlaq established a department of agriculture and canals
Balban introduced the theory of "narcotic kingship" / divine right of kings

questions.explanation:
Statement A is INCORRECT: coins called "sikka" were issued in Delhi from much earlier — Iltutmish issued the first silver tanka and introduced a standard Sultanate coinage, and copper "jital" coins were struck even earlier. Alauddin Khalji did not issue the first sikka; he reformed and standardised the currency during his market-control drive, but he was not its originator. Statements B, C and D are all correct: Muhammad bin Tughlaq's token (copper) currency had to be withdrawn after widespread forgery and public rejection; Firoz Shah Tughlaq set up a department of agriculture, dug canals and founded many towns; and Balban elevated royal pomp and the theory of "narcotic kingship" (divine right) to strengthen monarchical authority.

**Trap:** Students know Alauddin Khalji for currency-related actions, but those were reforms of an existing system, not its invention. Recognising Iltutmish as the founder of the Sultanate's standard coinage is the key to spotting the wrong statement.

questions.subject: history
questions.question: Which of the following correctly matches a Sultan with an event?

options.text: Muhammad bin Tughlaq — founded Hauz Khas
Qutb-ud-din Aibak — started construction of Qutub Minar

questions.explanation:
Qutb-ud-din Aibak began construction of the Qutub Minar at Mehrauli, Delhi, in 1199 CE (and the Quwwat-ul-Islam mosque), and Iltutmish completed the Minar and added further storeys. The Quwwat-ul-Islam mosque was begun by Aibak, not Alauddin Khalji (option B swaps the builder). Hauz Khas as the famous complex (madrasa, mosque and tomb) was developed later — the tank was excavated under Alauddin Khalji as Hauz-i-Alai, but the surviving complex is essentially Firoz Shah Tughlaq's work, not Muhammad bin Tughlaq's (so option A is wrong). The Iqta system is most often credited to Iltutmish, not "introduced" here as a special novelty of his; it was shaped by him but his pairing with Aibak/Qutub Minar makes option C the cleanest match.

**Trap:** Options A and B both shuffle correct attributes across wrong rulers, the typical way such match questions test students who half-remember the attributions.

questions.subject: history
questions.question:
Match the following:

| Sultan | Event |
|---|---|
| 1. Iltutmish | a. Introduced Iqta system |
| 2. Balban | b. Banned music and wine at court |
| 3. Muhammad bin Tughlaq | c. Token currency |
questions.explanation:
Iltutmish (r. 1211-1236 CE) refined and gave the Iqta (military land-revenue) system its classic, institutional form in the Delhi Sultanate (1-a). Balban, following Persian court models, imposed strict discipline at his court — banning music, wine, levity and other forms of indulgence to project royal gravity (2-b). Muhammad bin Tughlaq (r. 1325-1351 CE) introduced the ambitious token (copper) currency, pegged to the silver tanka, which had to be withdrawn after forgery and public unrest (3-c). All three pairings in option A are historically correct.

**Trap:** Option B misplaces the Iqta; option C assigns the token currency to Balban (it was Muhammad bin Tughlaq, not Balban); option D scrambles all three.

questions.subject: history
questions.question: The Sultan who shifted his capital from Delhi to Daulatabad was:
questions.explanation:
Muhammad bin Tughlaq (r. 1325-1351 CE) ordered the transfer of his capital from Delhi to Daulatabad (modern Aurangabad in the Deccan) around 1326-1327 CE, supposedly to safeguard against Mongol raids and to control the south better. The forced march of Delhi's populace southward caused immense suffering and the experiment failed; the capital was eventually moved back. Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq, his father, founded the Tughlaqabad city near Delhi; Alauddin Khalji was based in Delhi; Firoz Shah Tughlaq also ruled from Delhi (with a brief sojourn at Jaunpur).

**Trap:** Distractors A, B and D were all real Delhi-based Sultans, but only Muhammad bin Tughlaq made the dramatic capital-shift to Daulatabad.

questions.subject: history
questions.question:
Arrange in chronological order:

1. Slave Dynasty
2. Khilji Dynasty
3. Tughlaq Dynasty
4. Sayyid Dynasty
5. Lodi Dynasty
questions.explanation:
The correct chronological order of the five dynasties of the Delhi Sultanate is:

1. Slave (Mamluk) Dynasty (1206-1290 CE)
2. Khilji Dynasty (1290-1320 CE)
3. Tughlaq Dynasty (1320-1414 CE)
4. Sayyid Dynasty (1414-1451 CE)
5. Lodi Dynasty (1451-1526 CE), ending at Panipat (1526).

Option B reverses Slave and Khilji; option C places Lodi before Tughlaq; option D places Tughlaq before Khilji — all three errors violate the well-established chronology.

**Trap:** The Sayyid and Lodi dynasties were both short 15th-century lines and are easy to swap. Remember that the Lodi Dynasty, though short, is the LAST dynasty before the Sultanate ended.

questions.subject: history
questions.question:
Consider the statements:

1. The Delhi Sultanate reached its territorial peak under Alauddin Khalji.
2. Balban's "blood and iron" policy strengthened the frontier.
3. The Sultanate bureaucracy used Persian as its court language.

Which are correct?
questions.explanation:
All three statements are correct. (1) Under Alauddin Khalji the Sultanate stretched from the edge of the Himalayas in the north to the far south (Tamil country), covering its greatest land area. (2) Ghiyasuddin and especially Balban followed a "blood and iron" policy on the north-western frontier, dealing firmly with Mongol incursions and restoring internal order by harsh punishments. (3) Persian was the official court and administrative language of the Delhi Sultanate (and of the Mughals after them), used for official records, farmans and literature; the Sultanate bureaucracy was modelled on Turko-Persian lines.

**Trap:** Statement 1 is sometimes downplayed because Alauddin's market reforms are more famous than his conquests; yet his territorial reach was the Sultanate's largest. Statement 3's Persian is sometimes confused with Arabic — but Persian, not Arabic, was the working language of the chancery.

questions.subject: history
questions.question: The "Hauz Khas" complex (tank, mosque, madrasa, tombs) as it stands today was essentially built by:
questions.explanation:
The Hauz Khas complex in its surviving form was built by Firoz Shah Tughlaq (r. 1351-1388 CE). Firoz Shah re-excavated and enlarged the old water tank that Alauddin Khalji had originally dug as Hauz-i-Alai to supply water to the Siri Fort area, and around it built the grand madrasa, the mosque, his own tomb complex and the pavilions that survive today. Alauddin Khalji therefore started the tank but did not build the famous Hauz Khas buildings; Aibak predates the whole site; Sikandar Lodi built nothing here.

**Trap:** Alauddin Khalji's Hauz-i-Alai (the original reservoir) and Firoz Shah's Hauz Khas (the complex around it) are easily confused because the tank is the same piece of water. The buildings around it, however, are Firoz Shah's work.

questions.subject: history
questions.question: The Vijayanagara Empire was founded in 1336 CE by:
questions.explanation:
The Vijayanagara Empire was founded in 1336 CE by two brothers, Harihara I and Bukka I, initially with support and encouragement from the Sangama clan. Tradition holds that they were inspired/guided by the sage Vidyaranya to set up a new Hindu kingdom in the south as a bulwark against the Deccan sultanates. Krishnadevaraya (r. 1509-1529 CE) was the empire's most famous ruler but came much later. Prataparudra was a ruler of the Gajapati dynasty of Odisha. Saluva Narasimha was a later Vijayanagara king who founded the Saluva dynasty within the empire.

**Trap:** Distractor A (Krishnadevaraya) is the empire's most celebrated ruler, but he is the empire's great ruler, not its founder. Prataparudra and Saluva Narasimha are real Deccan-era rulers but are unrelated to the founding moment.
questions.wikilink: [[../../history/13 - Vijayanagara and Bahmani Kingdom.md#Content|Vijayanagara and Bahmani Kingdom — source chapter]]

questions.subject: history
questions.question: The Bahmani Kingdom was founded by:
questions.explanation:
The Bahmani Kingdom (also called the Bahmani Sultanate) was founded in 1347 CE by Ala-ud-din Hasan Bahman Shah, popularly known as Hasan Gangu, who broke away from the Delhi Sultanate and established an independent Muslim state in the Deccan with its capital at Gulbarga. Mahmud Gawan was a famous Bahmani vizier much later, not its founder. Muhammad Shah I and Ahmad Shah Wali were later Bahmani sultans who moved the capital to Bidar and presided over the kingdom's decline.

**Trap:** All four names are real Bahmani-era figures, but only Hasan Gangu is the dynasty's founder; the others held power long after the founding moment.
questions.wikilink: [[../../history/13 - Vijayanagara and Bahmani Kingdom.md#Content|Vijayanagara and Bahmani Kingdom — source chapter]]

questions.subject: history
questions.question: The Bahmani capital was shifted from Gulbarga to Bidar by:
questions.explanation:
Ahmad Shah Wali (Ahmad Shah I Bahmani, r. 1422-1435 CE) shifted the Bahmani capital from Gulbarga to Bidar around 1427-1428 CE because Bidar offered a more defensible hill-fort position and was better suited to project power across the Deccan. Ala-ud-din Hasan had originally founded the kingdom with Gulbarga as its capital; Mahmud Gawan was a vizier, not a sultan; Muhammad Shah I (Muhammad Shah Lashkari) came later and is associated with Gawan's execution.

**Trap:** Muhammad Shah I (option D) is associated with other dramatic Bahmani events (Mahmud Gawan's execution) but not the capital shift. Hasan Gangu (option A) is the dynasty's founder and is firmly tied to Gulbarga, not Bidar.
questions.wikilink: [[../../history/13 - Vijayanagara and Bahmani Kingdom.md#Content|Vijayanagara and Bahmani Kingdom — source chapter]]

questions.subject: history
questions.question: The capital of the Vijayanagara Empire was:
questions.explanation:
The imperial capital of the Vijayanagara Empire was the city of Vijayanagara on the south bank of the Tungabhadra river, whose ruins lie in and around present-day Hampi (a UNESCO World Heritage Site in Karnataka). Madurai was the base of the earlier Pandyan kingdom and a region the Vijayanagara rulers controlled but never made their main capital. Tanjore (Thanjavur) was the centre of the Chola power and later a Nayaka kingdom. Mysore became a major princely state only in the post-Vijayanagara period under the Wodeyars.

**Trap:** Madurai, Tanjore and Mysore are all famous south-Indian centres but were not the Vijayanagara capital; students often confuse regional power centres with the imperial capital.
questions.wikilink: [[../../history/13 - Vijayanagara and Bahmani Kingdom.md#Content|Vijayanagara and Bahmani Kingdom — source chapter]]

questions.subject: history
questions.question: A student reads that a Vijayanagara king wrote the Telugu poem Amuktamalyada, maintained diplomatic relations with the Portuguese, and bore the titles "Andhra Bhoja" and "Gajapati Trayambaka". The king being described is:
questions.explanation:
Krishnadevaraya (r. 1509-1529 CE), the most celebrated Vijayanagara ruler, authored the Telugu poem Amuktamalyada (a devotional work on Lord Venkateshwara), was the first major Indian king to welcome and engage with Portuguese envoys (including Domingo Paes and Barbosa), and was honoured by the titles "Andhra Bhoja" (a Bhoja-like patron of Telugu learning) and "Gajapati Trayambaka" (after his victories over the Gajapati rulers of Odisha). Bukka I co-founded the empire in 1336; Devaraya II was a 15th-century Vijayanagara ruler who fought the Bahmanis; Rama Raya was the regent/minister in the 1540s who effectively ran the empire and fell at Talikota.

**Trap:** Bukka I, Devaraya II and Rama Raya were all real Vijayanagara-era figures with military roles, but only Krishnadevaraya combines the literary (Amuktamalyada), diplomatic (Portuguese) and titular (Andhra Bhoja/Gajapati Trayambaka) clues.
questions.wikilink: [[../../history/13 - Vijayanagara and Bahmani Kingdom.md#Content|Vijayanagara and Bahmani Kingdom — source chapter]]

questions.subject: history
questions.question: Which battle marked the decisive defeat of Vijayanagara by the Deccan Sultanates in 1565?
questions.explanation:
The Battle of Talikota (also known as the Battle of Rakkasa-Tangadi), fought in January 1565 near the village of Talikota on the Krishna river, saw a combined army of the five Deccan Sultanates (Bijapur, Golconda, Ahmadnagar, Bidar and Berar) decisively defeat the Vijayanagara forces under Rama Raya. The defeat led to the sack and ruin of the city of Vijayanagara/Hampi and the end of Vijayanagara as a great imperial power. The Battle of Khanwa (1527) was Babur vs Rana Sanga; the First Battle of Panipat (1526) ended the Delhi Sultanate; the Battle of Plassey (1757) established British power in Bengal.

**Trap:** Distractors B, C and D are all famous Indian battles, but none involved the Deccan Sultanates or Vijayanagara.
questions.wikilink: [[../../history/13 - Vijayanagara and Bahmani Kingdom.md#Content|Vijayanagara and Bahmani Kingdom — source chapter]]

questions.subject: history
questions.question: The Portuguese traveller Domingo Paes visited the Vijayanagara court of:
questions.explanation:
Domingo Paes, a Portuguese horse-trader and chronicler, visited the Vijayanagara capital during the reign of Krishnadevaraya (around 1520 CE) and left a vivid account of the city, court and the king's personality. His description, together with that of Duarte Barbosa, is one of the most important eyewitness sources for Vijayanagara's glory before Talikota. Bukka I ruled in the 14th century, well before any Portuguese presence in India. Devaraya I was a 15th-century Vijayanagara king. Sadasiva Raya ruled in the 1540s-1560s (with Rama Raya as regent) but is not the king Paes described.

**Trap:** Distractors A, B and D are all real Vijayanagara rulers, but the Portuguese chroniclers were contemporaries of Krishnadevaraya, not the earlier or later rulers.
questions.wikilink: [[../../history/13 - Vijayanagara and Bahmani Kingdom.md#Content|Vijayanagara and Bahmani Kingdom — source chapter]]

questions.subject: history
questions.question:
Match the following:

| Ruler | Event |
|---|---|
| 1. Krishnadevaraya | a. Wrote Amuktamalyada |
| 2. Sadasiva Raya | b. Deposed by Rama Raya |
| 3. Rama Raya | c. The real power behind the throne in the 1540s |
questions.explanation:
(1-a) Krishnadevaraya is the author of the Telugu poem Amuktamalyada. (2-b) Sadasiva Raya, the nominal ruler of the empire in the late 1540s-1560s, was sidelined and effectively deposed by his regent Rama Raya, who ran the empire and commanded the army at Talikota. (3-c) Rama Raya (also called Rama or Ramaraja of the Aravidu line) was the all-powerful regent behind Sadasiva Raya's throne from the mid-1540s onward. All three pairings in option A are correct; options B, C and D each scramble at least one pairing.

**Trap:** Option D reverses the roles of Sadasiva Raya and Rama Raya, which is exactly the swap students make when they confuse the nominal king with the de facto ruler.
questions.wikilink: [[../../history/13 - Vijayanagara and Bahmani Kingdom.md#Content|Vijayanagara and Bahmani Kingdom — source chapter]]

questions.subject: history
questions.question: Mahmud Gawan, a famous Bahmani vizier, was executed by:
questions.explanation:
Mahmud Gawan (also called Mahmud Gavan), a Persian nobleman who served the Bahmani sultans as a brilliant administrator, general and patron of learning, was executed in 1481 CE by Muhammad Shah III (Muhammad Shah Lashkari) on trumped-up charges of treason after falling out with court factions hostile to foreign (Afaqi) ministers. Ahmad Shah Wali had moved the capital to Bidar but was long past the throne when Gawan fell. Hasan Gangu had founded the Bahmani state in 1347, more than a century earlier. Hussain Nizam Shah was the founder of the post-Bahmani Ahmadnagar Sultanate, not a Bahmani sultan.

**Trap:** Distractors A, C and D are all real Bahmani/Deccan-era figures but each belongs to a different era; only Muhammad Shah III was the sultan on the throne at the time of Gawan's fall.
questions.wikilink: [[../../history/13 - Vijayanagara and Bahmani Kingdom.md#Content|Vijayanagara and Bahmani Kingdom — source chapter]]

questions.subject: history
questions.question:
Arrange in chronological order:

1. Founding of Vijayanagara
2. Founding of Bahmani Kingdom
3. Formation of the five Deccan Sultanates
4. Battle of Talikota (1565)
questions.explanation:
The correct chronological order is:

1. Founding of Vijayanagara (1336 CE) by Harihara I and Bukka I.
2. Founding of the Bahmani Kingdom (1347 CE) by Hasan Gangu, breaking from Delhi.
3. Formation of the five Deccan Sultanates (Ahmadnagar, Bijapur, Golconda, Berar and Bidar) around the 1490s as the Bahmani state broke apart under Afaqi-Deccani feuds and weak successors.
4. Battle of Talikota (1565 CE), in which the combined Deccan sultans routed the Vijayanagara forces under Rama Raya.

Option B reverses Vijayanagara and Bahmani (placing Bahmani before 1336); option C places Talikota before the sultanates formed; option D reverses the entire sequence.

**Trap:** The common error is treating Bahmani (1347) as earlier than Vijayanagara (1336) because the Bahmanis were Islamic and predate, in popular memory, the "Hindu revival" of Vijayanagara; in fact, Vijayanagara was founded eleven years before the Bahmani state.
questions.wikilink: [[../../history/13 - Vijayanagara and Bahmani Kingdom.md#Content|Vijayanagara and Bahmani Kingdom — source chapter]]

questions.subject: history
questions.question:
Consider the statements:

1. The Vijayanagara Empire had a powerful navy that controlled the Bay of Bengal trade.
2. Krishnadevaraya defeated the Gajapatis of Odisha and the Bahmani Sultans in campaigns that made the empire the dominant power in South India.
3. The ruins of Hampi today are a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

Which are correct?
questions.explanation:
Statements 2 and 3 are correct. (2) Krishnadevaraya's military campaigns against the Gajapati rulers of Odisha (consolidating control over the eastern coast up to the Godavari-Krishna doab) and against the Bahmani/Deccan sultans (most famously the campaign over Raichur) made the Vijayanagara Empire the dominant power in South India during his reign. (3) The ruins of Hampi, the capital city of Vijayanagara, were inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1986, covering the Sacred Centre, royal and sacred complexes, and over 1,600 surviving remains.

Statement 1 is incorrect or at best debatable: the Vijayanagara Empire was essentially a land-based power whose economy depended on agricultural surplus and inland trade; its maritime activity was limited and it did not "control the Bay of Bengal trade" in the way that, for example, the Cholas or later the European trading companies did.

**Trap:** Statement 1 is the kind of assertion students half-accept because the Cholas (just before) had a famous navy; the Vijayanagara Empire, however, was a successor inland power, not a maritime one.
questions.wikilink: [[../../history/13 - Vijayanagara and Bahmani Kingdom.md#Content|Vijayanagara and Bahmani Kingdom — source chapter]]

questions.subject: history
questions.question: The Bahmani Sultanate gave way to the five Deccan Sultanates primarily because of:

options.text: Defeat by the Vijayanagara empire at Talikota
Internal wars of succession and weakening of central authority
Conversion of the Bahmanis to Christianity

questions.explanation:
The Bahmani Sultanate fractured into the five Deccan Sultanates (Bijapur, Golconda, Ahmadnagar, Berar and Bidar) during the 1490s because of internal decay: bitter Afaqi (foreign, mainly Persian/Arab) vs Deccani (local, Indian-born Muslim) factionalism, weak and short-reigned sultans, succession wars among the governors, and the collapse of central authority. These centrifugal forces broke the state apart before the end of the 15th century. The Battle of Talikota (1565 CE) happened AFTER this breakup, when the now-independent sultanates combined against Vijayanagara, so option A confuses cause and effect. There was no Bahmani conversion to Christianity (D), and Mughal invasions of the Deccan (C) occurred only in the 17th century under Akbar, Shah Jahan and Aurangzeb, well after the Bahmani state was gone.

**Trap:** Option A is the most attractive wrong answer because Talikota is the most famous Vijayanagara-vs-sultanates battle; but the sultanates were already independent states by the time of Talikota, so the breakup cannot have been caused by it.
questions.wikilink: [[../../history/13 - Vijayanagara and Bahmani Kingdom.md#Content|Vijayanagara and Bahmani Kingdom — source chapter]]

questions.subject: history
questions.question: The founder of the Mughal Empire was:
questions.explanation:
The Mughal Empire was founded by Zahir-ud-din Muhammad Babur (r. 1526-1530 CE), a Timurid prince from Central Asia who defeated Ibrahim Lodi at the First Battle of Panipat (1526 CE) and then defeated Rana Sanga at the Battle of Khanwa (1527 CE). Humayun (option B) was Babur's son and the second Mughal emperor but lost the empire for a while to Sher Shah Suri. Akbar (option C) was the third and most famous Mughal emperor but he inherited the throne as a boy in 1556 CE, three decades after the founding. Sher Shah Suri (option D) is often confused with the founder because his brief interlude (1540-1555 CE) interrupted Mughal rule, but he was an Afghan, not a Mughal, and his dynasty was the Sur, not the Mughal.

**Trap:** Option B (Humayun) is the easiest wrong answer because the Mughal Empire is sometimes loosely said to have been "
e-established" by him; but Humayun only restored the dynasty after losing it, he did not found it. Option D (Sher Shah Suri) is the trap for students who confuse the famous "interlude" ruler with the actual founder.

questions.subject: history
questions.question: The Battle of Khanwa (1527) was fought between Babur and:
questions.explanation:
The Battle of Khanwa (17 March 1527 CE) was fought between Babur and Rana Sanga, the ruler of Mewar, near the village of Khanwa in present-day Rajasthan. Babur's victory decisively broke the Rajput confederacy's resistance and secured Mughal control over much of north India. Ibrahim Lodi (option A) was Babur's opponent at the First Battle of Panipat (1526 CE), not Khanwa. Sher Shah Suri (option C) defeated Babur's son Humayun at the Battle of Kannauj (1540 CE) and is associated with the Mughal interlude, not with Khanwa. Hemu (option D) was a general who briefly defeated the Mughals and crowned himself at Panipat in 1556 CE, almost three decades after Khanwa.

**Trap:** Option A (Ibrahim Lodi) is the most tempting wrong answer because Panipat 1526 and Khanwa 1527 happened in consecutive years under Babur and are often taught together; students must remember that Panipat was against the Delhi Sultanate while Khanwa was against the Rajputs.

questions.subject: history
questions.question: Akbar's policy of "Sulh-i-Kul" (universal tolerance) is associated with:
questions.explanation:
Sulh-i-Kul (literally "peace with all" or universal tolerance) was Akbar's policy of religious pluralism, cultivated through interfaith dialogue at the Ibadat Khana (House of Worship) at Fatehpur Sikri from 1575 CE onwards, and culminating in the syncretic Din-i-Ilahi (the "Divine Faith") that Akbar promulgated around 1582 CE. Military conquests (option A) were a parallel and earlier activity, not the basis of Sulh-i-Kul. Todar Mal's land revenue reforms (option C) were a fiscal-administrative innovation, unrelated to religious policy. The mansabdari system (option D) was Akbar's military-administrative ranking system for nobles and officers, again a different domain.

**Trap:** Options C and D are both real Akbar-era reforms, so students who know Akbar but blur his many policies together can confuse which reform belongs to which category. The unique marker of Sulh-i-Kul is its religious, not fiscal or military, content.

questions.subject: history
questions.question: Aurangzeb reimposed Jizya in:
questions.explanation:
Aurangzeb reimposed the Jizya (a poll tax on non-Muslims, abolished earlier by Akbar in 1564 CE) in 1679 CE. This was one of the most contested acts of his reign and is widely regarded as a turning point in Mughal-Rajput and Mughal-Maratha relations. Option A (1564 CE) is the year Akbar ABOLISHED the Jizya and is the trap for students who confuse who abolished/re-imposed it. Option B (1659 CE) is the year Aurangzeb executed his brother Dara Shukoh and consolidated power at the start of his reign, not the year of the Jizya. Option D (1707 CE) is the year of Aurangzeb's death.

**Trap:** Option A is the strongest distractor because Akbar's abolition (1564) and Aurangzeb's reimposition (1679) are mirror-image events; the question deliberately asks about REIMPOSITION, so the answer must be the later date.

questions.subject: history
questions.question: A student reads that an interlude of Mughal rule in India was led by an Afghan who built the Grand Trunk Road, introduced the silver "Rupia", and was eventually defeated by Humayun. The ruler being described is:
questions.explanation:
The ruler described is Sher Shah Suri (Farid Khan, r. 1540-1545 CE), an Afghan of the Sur dynasty who briefly displaced Humayun and ruled from Delhi and Agra. Sher Shah is famous for: (i) rebuilding and extending the Grand Trunk Road from the Indus to Bengal, (ii) issuing the silver "Rupiya" coin that became the ancestor of the modern rupee, (iii) introducing a survey-based land revenue system that later influenced Todar Mal's reforms, and (iv) defeating Humayun at Kannauj in 1540 CE before Humayun returned to reconquer Delhi in 1555 CE. Babur (option B) founded the Mughal dynasty and was not Afghan. Bairam Khan (option C) was a Persian-origin regent who helped the young Akbar, not an interlude ruler. Ibrahim Lodi (option D) was the last Lodi Sultan defeated by Babur at Panipat in 1526 CE.

**Trap:** Option B (Babur) is the trap for students who confuse "Mughal founder" with "interlude ruler"; the question explicitly mentions the interlude period and Humayun's defeat, both of which point to the Sur interlude.

questions.subject: history
questions.question: Which of the following is INCORRECT about Akbar's administration?

options.text: The Ibadat Khana was at Fatehpur Sikri
Todar Mal's bandobast was a land-revenue settlement

questions.explanation:
Statement D is INCORRECT because Akbar abolished the Jizya in 1564 CE, not in 1679 CE. The year 1679 CE is when Aurangzeb REIMPOSED the Jizya; mixing up the two rulers and the two events makes this the wrong option. Statements A, B and C are all correct: the Ibadat Khana was indeed constructed at Fatehpur Sikri in 1575 CE; the Mansabdari system organized officers into 33 grades (called zat and sawar ranks); and Todar Mal's " andobast" (settled assessment) of 1580-1582 CE was Akbar's famous land revenue reform based on careful crop and area measurement.

**Trap:** Option D is engineered to confuse the year Akbar abolished the Jizya with the year Aurangzeb reimposed it. Students who know that "	he Jizya was abolished by Akbar" but confuse the date will pick D as the answer; the date 1679 is the giveaway that this is the INCORRECT statement.

questions.subject: history
questions.question: Who was the last Mughal emperor?
questions.explanation:
Bahadur Shah Zafar II (r. 1837-1857 CE) was the last Mughal emperor. He was a titular ruler confined by the British to the Red Fort at Delhi and was deposed and exiled to Rangoon (Burma) after the 1857 uprising, in which he was proclaimed a symbolic leader of the revolt. He died in 1862 CE. Akbar II (option B) was the second-to-last emperor (r. 1806-1837 CE) and Bahadur Shah Zafar II's father. Aurangzeb (option C) died in 1707 CE, more than a century before the end of Mughal power. Bahadur Shah I (option D, also called Muazzam, r. 1707-1712 CE) was Aurangzeb's immediate successor and the first emperor after the long Maratha-Deccan wars.

**Trap:** Option C (Aurangzeb) is the most attractive wrong answer because Aurangzeb's death (1707 CE) is widely cited as the start of Mughal decline; but he was not the LAST emperor, only the last of the strong "Great Mughals." Option B (Akbar II) is the trap for students who know the next-to-last emperor but not the very last.

questions.subject: history
questions.question:
Match the following Mughal rulers with their associated works:

| Ruler | Work / Building |
|---|---|
| 1. Akbar | a. Taj Mahal (commission) |
| 2. Shah Jahan | b. Agra Fort, Fatehpur Sikri |
| 3. Babur | c. Baburnama |
questions.explanation:
The correct matching is 1-b, 2-a, 3-c. Akbar (1) is associated with Agra Fort (the red sandstone fort at Agra) and Fatehpur Sikri (the imperial city he built and largely abandoned), which is option b. Shah Jahan (2) commissioned the Taj Mahal at Agra as a tomb for his wife Mumtaz Mahal, which is option a. Babur (3) authored the Baburnama, his memoirs in Chagatai Turkish, which is option c. Options A and D misalign one or more rulers with their monuments or works.

**Trap:** Option A swaps Akbar with Shah Jahan in students' memories because Shah Jahan is more famous for architecture; students who remember "Akbar -> Agra Fort" and "Shah Jahan -> Taj Mahal" but forget the Baburnama column can pick A. Option C pairs Babur with Taj Mahal (clearly wrong) but otherwise mixes the pairings.

questions.subject: history
questions.question: The Deccan policies of Aurangzeb ultimately:

options.text: Consolidated Mughal control and yielded a stable empire
Drained the treasury and exposed the north to Maratha attacks
Brought peace with the Marathas through treaties
Led to a complete annexation of the Maratha kingdom

questions.explanation:
Aurangzeb's long Deccan campaigns (1681-1707 CE), especially against the Marathas under Shivaji and his successors Sambhaji and Rajaram, drained the imperial treasury, tied down the best Mughal armies far from the north, and exposed northern India to Jat, Sikh and later Rajput-Maratha incursions. The Marathas were never fully defeated; they adopted guerrilla tactics, and by the time of Aurangzeb's death (1707 CE) Mughal control of the Deccan was nominal at best. Option A is the opposite of the historical outcome. Option C is incorrect because Aurangzeb refused to treat the Marathas as legitimate political equals and never made a lasting peace with them. Option D is incorrect because Aurangzeb captured and executed Sambhaji but never fully annexed Maratha territory; Shivaji's successors continued the fight.

**Trap:** Option A is tempting if students remember that Aurangzeb briefly captured Maratha strongholds; but the long-term effect of his Deccan campaigns was exhaustion, not consolidation. Option D is the trap for students who over-simplify Aurangzeb's campaigns as a "ictory over the Marathas."

questions.subject: history
questions.question:
Arrange the following in chronological order:

1. Babur's invasion
2. Sher Shah Suri's interlude
3. Akbar's accession
4. Aurangzeb's death
questions.explanation:
The correct chronological order is 1 -> 2 -> 3 -> 4. (1) Babur's invasion and the founding of the Mughal Empire occurred in 1526 CE with the First Battle of Panipat. (2) Sher Shah Suri's interlude ran from 1540 to 1555 CE, after he defeated Humayun at Kannauj. (3) Akbar acceded to the Mughal throne in 1556 CE (with Bairam Khan as regent) and ruled until 1605 CE. (4) Aurangzeb died in 1707 CE after his long Deccan campaigns. Option A reverses (2) and (3), placing Akbar's accession before the Sur interlude. Option C scrambles all four events. Option D places Aurangzeb's death before Akbar's accession, which is impossible.

**Trap:** Option A is the most attractive wrong answer because students often forget that Sher Shah's interlude (1540-1555 CE) actually came BETWEEN Babur (1526) and Akbar (1556); they assume the dynasty passed smoothly from Babur to Humayun to Akbar.

questions.subject: history
questions.question:
Consider the statements:

1. Akbar's Rajput policy was based on matrimonial alliances and strategic incorporation.
2. Shah Jahan's reign is called the "Golden Age of the Mughals" for architecture.
3. Aurangzeb's religious policies made him the most popular Mughal emperor with the people.

Which are correct?
questions.explanation:
Statements 1 and 2 are correct; statement 3 is INCORRECT. Akbar's Rajput policy was indeed a policy of matrimonial alliances (he married Jodha Bai / Harkha Bai of Amer, plus other Rajput princesses) and strategic incorporation of Rajput chiefs as trusted Mughal nobles and governors; this pacified the Rajputana region and produced long-lasting alliances. Shah Jahan's reign (1628-1658 CE) is widely known as the "Golden Age of the Mughals" for architecture because of the Taj Mahal, the Red Fort at Delhi, the Jama Masjid, the Moti Masjid, and the Peacock Throne; the empire was at its largest territorial extent and richest in this period. Statement 3 is INCORRECT because Aurangzeb's religious policies (reimposition of Jizya in 1679 CE, destruction of temples, banning of music at court, etc.) made him UNPOPULAR with the Rajputs, Marathas, Sikhs and a large section of the Hindu population, contributing to revolts that weakened the empire.

**Trap:** Option D (1, 2 and 3) is the trap for students who know that Shah Jahan was architecturally glorious and assume the "most popular emperor" claim must therefore also be true. Option B flips the correctness and includes the false statement 3.

questions.subject: history
questions.question: Who composed the "Akbarnama" and "Ain-i-Akbari"?
questions.explanation:
Abul Fazl (1551-1602 CE), the court historian and one of Akbar's "Nine Jewels" (Navaratnas), was the author of both the Akbarnama (a three-volume chronicle of Akbar's reign) and the Ain-i-Akbari (the third volume of the Akbarnama, which serves as a detailed administrative and cultural manual of Akbar's empire). Faizi (option B) was Abul Fazl's elder brother, also a Navaratna, who translated Sanskrit works into Persian and was a poet, but he did not compose these specific texts. Birbal (option C) was another Navaratna, famous as a witty courtier and military commander, but not a historian. Tansen (option D) was the legendary court musician, also a Navaratna, but composed dhrupads and ragas, not historical chronicles.

**Trap:** Options B, C and D are all "Nine Jewels" of Akbar's court, so all four answer choices are real Mughal-era figures associated with Akbar; the question requires students to identify the specific scholar-historian among the Navaratnas. Students who know the phrase "Nine Jewels" but not each member's work will be misled.

questions.subject: history
questions.question: The Maratha king Shivaji was crowned Chhatrapati at:
questions.explanation:
Shivaji was formally crowned Chhatrapati (a sovereign Hindu royal title meaning "`shadow of the supreme`") on 6 June 1674 CE at Raigad Fort, the hill capital he had wrested from the Sultanate of Bijapur. The coronation was performed by the Brahmin scholar Gagabhatt, who was specifically summoned from Varanasi to give it ritual legitimacy. Pune (option B) was Shivaji's later administrative center under the Peshwas but never the coronation site. Torna (option C) was Shivaji's first major fort conquest (1646 CE) at age 16, important but a capture, not a coronation. Pratapgad (option D) was the fort where the famous 1659 encounter with Afzal Khan took place, which is also wrongly conflated with the coronation date.

**Trap:** Options C and D both name real Shivaji-era forts associated with real Shivaji events (the first fort capture and the Afzal Khan encounter respectively), which makes them the strongest distractors; students must keep the coronation separate from these other landmarks and remember 1674 at Raigad.

questions.subject: history
questions.question: The Treaty of Purandar (1665) was signed between Shivaji and:
questions.explanation:
The Treaty of Purandar (June 1665 CE) was signed between Shivaji and Mirza Raja Jai Singh I, the Mughal general (and Rajput noble of Amber/Jaipur) sent by Aurangzeb to subdue the Marathas after Shaista Khan's failed campaigns. Under the treaty, Shivaji ceded 23 of his 35 forts to the Mughals, retained 12, and agreed to serve the Mughal emperor as a vassal. Aurangzeb (option A) was the Mughal emperor but did not personally negotiate at Purandar; his representative Jai Singh did. Dara Shukoh (option B) was Aurangzeb's elder brother, defeated at the War of Succession in 1658 CE and dead by 1659 CE - well before Purandar. Shaista Khan (option D) was the Mughal governor of the Deccan whom Shivaji had famously raided in 1663 CE at Pune (the famous night attack on Shaista Khan), but he was not the treaty signatory.

**Trap:** Option A is the strongest distractor because Aurangzeb was the emperor on whose orders Jai Singh acted; students who remember only "`Mughal emperor`" but not the actual negotiator will pick A. Option D is the trap for students who confuse the famous 1663 Pune raid with the 1665 treaty.

questions.subject: history
questions.question: The Third Battle of Panipat (1761) was fought between Marathas and:
questions.explanation:
The Third Battle of Panipat (14 January 1761 CE) was fought between the Maratha Confederacy, led by Sadashivrao Bhau (with Vishwasrao and the Peshwa's son) along with Ibrahim Ali Gardi, and Ahmad Shah Abdali (also called Ahmad Shah Durrani), the Afghan ruler from Kabul, who was supported by Rohilla Afghans and the Nawab of Awadh, Shuja-ud-Daula. The battle was a catastrophic defeat for the Marathas and effectively halted their northward expansion. Option B (Abdali and the Nizam) is partially true in that the Nizam of Hyderabad, Nizam Ali (Salabat Jung), was on the Abdali side, but the core opposition to the Marathas was led by Abdali, not the Nizam. Hyder Ali (option C) was the ruler of Mysore in the south and was not involved at Panipat 1761. The British (option D) were not involved at the Third Battle of Panipat; their role in defeating the Marathas came in the three Anglo-Maratha Wars of 1775-1818 CE.

**Trap:** Option B is engineered to confuse students who remember that the Nizam also fought the Marathas at Kharda (1795); at Panipat 1761 the Nizam was only a secondary partner of Abdali, not the main opponent. Option D is the trap for students who conflate the post-1761 Anglo-Maratha wars with the earlier Panipat defeat.

questions.subject: history
questions.question: "Chauth" was a tax equal to:
questions.explanation:
Chauth (literally "`one-fourth`") was a protection/protection-cum-tribute tax levied by the Marathas, mainly the Peshwas and their sardars, equal to one-fourth (25%) of the land revenue of a given territory, collected from areas not directly under Maratha administration in return for "`protection`" from Maratha raids. Its companion levy was Sardeshmukhi, an additional 10% claimed from the same territories by the Maratha chieftain who held the sardeshmukhi (headship) right. Together, the "`Chauth-Sardeshmukhi`" became the financial backbone of the Maratha state and paralleled a military fiscal system. Option A (one-eighth) is wrong. Option C (half) is wrong and is the trap for students who assume a "`heavy tribute.`" Option D (one-tenth) is closer to Sardeshmukhi, the sister tax, not Chauth itself.

**Trap:** Option D is the strongest distractor because Sardeshmukhi (10%) was the parallel Maratha levy and students frequently confuse the two; the question specifies Chauth, which is specifically one-fourth. Option A is the trap for students who half-remember "`a small share of revenue`" without recalling it was 25%.

questions.subject: history
questions.question: A student reads that the Maratha revenue and military system was the "Chauth-Sardeshmukhi" with a parallel military finance through deshmukhs and watandars. The system being described is:

options.text: The mansabdari system of the Mughals

questions.explanation:
The system being described is the Maratha revenue-cum-military system, in which (i) Chauth (1/4 of land revenue) and Sardeshmukhi (an additional 1/10) were the two taxes collected by the Marathas from territories not directly under their administration; and (ii) deshmukhs and watandars (hereditary local officials holding watan/jagir lands) financed and provided the cavalry and infantry contingents that made up the Maratha army. The mansabdari system (option A) was the Mughal ranking system of nobles by zat and sawar ranks, not a tax levy. The iqta system (option C) was the Delhi Sultanate's land-revenue-cum-military assignment. The samanta system (option D) was the early medieval Indian practice of vassal chieftains paying tribute; it is conceptually related but refers to an earlier period and not to the specific Maratha combination.

**Trap:** Option A is tempting because the Mughals and Marathas co-existed and both had ranking systems, but mansabdari was specifically Mughal and did not feature Chauth-Sardeshmukhi. Option D is the trap for students who think all Indian "`vassal + tribute`" arrangements are the samanta system; the Maratha version is distinctive enough to have its own name.

questions.subject: history
questions.question:
Match the following:

| Peshwa | Associated event |
|---|---|
| 1. Balaji Vishwanath | a. Baji Rao I succeeded his father |
| 2. Baji Rao I | b. Treaty of Bassein |
| 3. Baji Rao II | c. Became Peshwa by eliminating rivals |
questions.explanation:
The correct matching is 1-c, 2-a, 3-b. Balaji Vishwanath (1), who became Peshwa in 1713 CE, is famous for becoming Peshwa by outmaneuvering and eliminating his rivals (notably Kanhoji Shirke and the influential Maratha noble families) and for being the father of the celebrated warrior Peshwa Baji Rao I; that rivalry-elimination is event c. Baji Rao I (2), who succeeded his father Balaji Vishwanath in 1720 CE and served until 1740 CE, was a brilliant military Peshwa who expanded Maratha influence across north India up to Delhi and into Rajasthan and Malwa; that direct father-to-son succession is event a. Baji Rao II (3), Peshwa from 1795 to 1818 CE, signed the Treaty of Bassein with the British in 1802 CE, an act that effectively made him a British client and began the end of Maratha independence; that is event b. Options B, C and D scramble one or more of these pairings.

**Trap:** Option D is the strongest trap because it puts Baji Rao II with the "`succeeded his father`" claim, which is confusing since Baji Rao II DID succeed his father (Raghunath Rao / Raghoba) but his more famous association is with Bassein, so the right pairing of 3 with b makes A correct. Option C scrambles all three pairings.

questions.subject: history
questions.question: After the Third Battle of Panipat (1761), the Maratha confederacy was reconstructed under whose leadership?
questions.explanation:
After the devastating Maratha defeat at the Third Battle of Panipat (1761 CE), the Maratha confederacy was reconstructed under the leadership of the young Peshwa Madhavrao I (Peshwa 1761-1772 CE), son of Balaji Bajirao (Nanasaheb) and grandson of Baji Rao I. Madhavrao restored Maratha finances, reasserted Peshwa authority over the fractious sardars (Holkar, Scindia, Bhonsle, Gaekwad), and recovered many of the territories lost at Panipat. Balaji Bajirao (Nanasaheb), option B, was Madhavrao's father but is associated with the period immediately before and during Panipat (he was Peshwa 1740-1761 CE and died shortly after the battle, reportedly of shock). Bajirao II (option C) was the last Peshwa (1795-1818 CE) who signed the Treaty of Bassein and lost the remaining Maratha independence. Mahadji Shinde (option D) was the Scindia chief who recovered Delhi for the Marathas in 1771 CE - an important action, but he served UNDER Madhavrao's broader reconstruction, not as the primary leader.

**Trap:** Option B is the strongest trap because Nanasaheb was the Peshwa at the time of Panipat; but the reconstruction after the defeat was led by his SON Madhavrao. Option D is the trap for students who remember Mahadji Shinde's dramatic recapture of Delhi in 1771 but forget that the broader confederacy-wide reconstruction was led by the Peshwa.

questions.subject: history
questions.question: Who among the following Peshwas signed the Treaty of Bassein (1802) with the British?
questions.explanation:
The Treaty of Bassein (also called the Treaty of Vasai, signed on 31 December 1802 CE) was signed between Baji Rao II (Peshwa 1795-1818 CE) and the British East India Company (represented by the Governor General, Lord Wellesley). Under its terms, Baji Rao II ceded territory and accepted a subsidiary alliance, which in effect made the Peshwa a British client and triggered the Second Anglo-Maratha War (1803-1805 CE). Balaji Vishwanath (option A) was the Peshwa who concluded the Treaty of Purandar-style settlements in the early 1700s and made the Peshwa hereditary, not Bassein. Baji Rao I (option B) was a famous military Peshwa (1720-1740 CE) who expanded Maratha power northward to Delhi and into Rajasthan and the Deccan, but lived a century before Bassein. Nana Sahib (option D) was the adopted son of Baji Rao II and led the 1857 rebellion at Kanpur, well after the Peshwa's downfall in 1818.

**Trap:** Option B (Baji Rao I) is the most attractive wrong answer because Baji Rao I is the most famous Peshwa and his name is associated with territorial expansion; but it was his descendant Baji Rao II who signed Bassein. Option A is the trap for students who confuse Balaji Vishwanath's earlier Purandar-era diplomacy with Baji Rao II's Bassein signing.

questions.subject: history
questions.question: Which of the following is INCORRECT about Shivaji's administration?

options.text: The "Ashtapradhan" was a council of eight ministers
The military was organized into infantry (Mavla), cavalry, and navy
Shivaji abolished the Hindu festival of Diwali

questions.explanation:
Statement D is INCORRECT: Shivaji did not abolish Diwali. Diwali is the Hindu festival of lights, celebrated across India, and was actively promoted by Shivaji; the very coronation at Raigad in 1674 CE was timed to coincide with a Hindu auspicious festival. Far from abolishing festivals, Shivaji used Hindu religious identity to mobilize the Maratha identity against Mughal pressure. Statements A, B and C are all correct: the Ashtapradhan was indeed a council of eight ministers headed by the Peshwa and others (Amatya, Sachiva, Mantri, Senapati, Sumant, Nyayadhish, Panditrao, and Dandadhikari); Shivaji's revenue system did include "`Kathi`" (a rough area measurement unit) and "`Ryotwari`" was the mode of settlement directly with the cultivator; and the Maratha military under Shivaji had Mavla infantry, the cavalry under his sardars (notably the "`Bargi`" or "`Silahdar`" horsemen), and a navy commanded by Kanhoji Angre and others.

**Trap:** Option D is designed to test whether students know that Shivaji was a champion of Hindu identity, not its opponent; the absurdity of "`abolished Diwali`" is the giveaway that this is the INCORRECT statement. Options A, B and C each contain real Maratha-administration terms.

questions.subject: history
questions.question:
Arrange in chronological order of Shivaji's life events:

1. Treaty of Purandar
2. Agra visit to Aurangzeb's court
3. Coronation at Raigad
4. Death
questions.explanation:
The correct chronological order of Shivaji's life events is 1 -> 2 -> 3 -> 4. (1) The Treaty of Purandar was signed on 11 June 1665 CE between Shivaji and Mirza Raja Jai Singh, under which Shivaji ceded 23 forts. (2) Shivaji's visit to Aurangzeb's court at Agra happened in 1666 CE, after he went ostensibly as a Mughal vassal and was placed under house arrest, escaping dramatically in a fruit basket. (3) The coronation at Raigad took place on 6 June 1674 CE. (4) Shivaji died on 3 April 1680 CE at Raigad. So the order is Purandar (1665) -> Agra visit (1666) -> Coronation (1674) -> Death (1680), which is option A. Option B places death before coronation, which is impossible. Option C swaps Purandar and the Agra visit. Option D begins with coronation, which is clearly wrong because both Purandar and Agra pre-date 1674.

**Trap:** Option C is the most attractive wrong answer because students may half-remember "`Shivaji went to Agra`" and "`Treaty of Purandar`" but reverse which came first; in fact, Purandar (1665) preceded the Agra visit (1666) by about a year. Option B is a memory slip that places death before coronation.

questions.subject: history
questions.question:
Consider the statements:

1. The Peshwas were originally Prime Ministers of the Maratha king, but became the de facto rulers.
2. The Battle of Kharda (1795) saw the Maratha Peshwa defeat the Nizam.
3. The Maratha confederacy was finally defeated by the British in the Third Anglo-Maratha War (1818).

Which are correct?
questions.explanation:
All three statements are correct. (1) The Peshwas were originally the Prime Ministers (literally "`foremost`" in Persian) under the Chhatrapati (Maratha king); over time, beginning with Balaji Vishwanath (1713 CE), the Peshwa became hereditary and from Baji Rao I onwards exercised de facto control over the Maratha state even though the Chhatrapati remained the nominal sovereign. (2) The Battle of Kharda (11 March 1795 CE) was fought between the forces of the Peshwa (under the broader Nana Fadnavis-led campaign and Baji Rao II's army) and the Nizam of Hyderabad; the Marathas won a decisive victory. (3) The Third Anglo-Maratha War (1817-1818 CE) culminated in the defeat of the Peshwa Baji Rao II at the Battle of Khadki and the Battle of Koregaon, the surrender of Baji Rao II, and the formal end of Maratha political power - the "`final defeat`" of the confederacy. Therefore, all three statements (1, 2, and 3) are correct, making option D the right answer.

**Trap:** Option A (1 and 2 only) and Option B (2 and 3 only) are both traps that omit one true statement; the test is whether students can verify all three independently. Option C is the trap for students who wrongly believe the confederacy ended earlier (e.g., at Bassein 1802 or after Panipat 1761) rather than at the Third Anglo-Maratha War 1818.

questions.subject: history
questions.question: The Maratha sardars under the Peshwas included:

options.text: The Scindias of Gwalior, Holkars of Indore, Gaekwads of Baroda, Bhonsles of Nagpur
The Rajputs of Amber, Jaipur, Mewar, Marwar
The Nawab-Wazirs of Awadh, Bengal, Arcot, Hyderabad

questions.explanation:
The five great Maratha sardar families (also called "`the five houses of the Maratha Confederacy`") were: (i) the Peshwas of Pune (the de facto prime ministers who led the state), (ii) the Scindias (Shindes) of Gwalior under Mahadji Shinde and Daulat Rao Scindia, (iii) the Holkars of Indore under Malhar Rao Holkar and Tukoji Holkar, (iv) the Gaekwads (Gaikwads) of Baroda under Damaji Rao Gaekwad and later Sayaji Rao, and (v) the Bhonsles of Nagpur under Raghoji Bhonsle and later Appa Sahib Bhonsle. So option A correctly lists four of the five major Maratha houses (excluding the Peshwas of Pune themselves). The Rajputs (option B) were a different warrior class and polity, mainly in Rajasthan. The Nawab-Wazirs (option C) were Muslim provincial rulers (Awadh, Bengal, etc.) and not Maratha sardars at all. The Sikh Misls (option D) were the 12 Sikh warrior bands of Punjab under Ranjit Singh's later unification - not Maratha.

**Trap:** Option B (Rajputs) is the strongest trap because Rajputana and Maratha territory overlapped (parts of Rajasthan were under Maratha Chauth by the 1750s) and the Rajputs are also a famous warrior class; but they were not Maratha sardars. Option C is the trap for students who confuse "`regional Indian rulers of the 18th century`" with Maratha houses.

questions.subject: history
questions.question: Which of the following saints is the founder of the Nathpanthi / Shaiva tradition that emphasised yoga?
questions.explanation:
Matsyendranath (also spelled Matsyendranatha) is regarded as the founder of the Nathpanthi tradition, a strand of Shaiva mysticism that placed strong emphasis on yoga, breath-control (pranayama) and the guru-disciple relationship. Ramanuja (option A) was a Vedantic philosopher and founder of Vishishtadvaita. Basavanna (option C) founded the Lingayat movement in 12th-century Karnataka. Kabir (option D) was a 15th-century north Indian sant-poet, not a Nathpanthi founder.

**Trap:** Ramanuja and Kabir are easy to confuse with Nathpanthi yogis because both emphasised devotion and a personal inner path. But yoga-centred Shaiva asceticism is the Nathpanthi hallmark associated with Matsyendranath and his disciple Gorakhnath.
questions.wikilink: [[../../history/16 - Bhakti and Sufi Movements.md#Content|Bhakti and Sufi Movements — source chapter]]

questions.subject: history
questions.question: Ramanuja's philosophical system is known as:
questions.explanation:
Ramanuja (trad. 1017-1137 CE), the foremost Srivaishnava theologian, propounded **Vishishtadvaita** (qualified non-dualism), which holds that Brahman, souls and the world are inseparable realities, like attributes of the one Being, while the world is real and grace (prapatti) is the path to liberation. Advaita (option A) is Shankara's non-dualism. Dvaita (option C) is Madhva's dualism. Shuddhadvaita (option D) is Vallabhacharya's "pure non-dualism".

**Trap:** All four options look similar because they end in "-dvaita", so reading the prefix matters: *Vishishta-* (qualified), *Shuddha-* (pure), *a-* (non-). A student who only remembers "Ramanuja = some kind of advaita" often picks A.
questions.wikilink: [[../../history/16 - Bhakti and Sufi Movements.md#Content|Bhakti and Sufi Movements — source chapter]]

questions.subject: history
questions.question: The Lingayat movement was founded by:
questions.explanation:
The Lingayat (also Lingayat/Virashaiva) movement was founded by Basavanna in the 12th century at Kalyana (in present-day Karnataka), the capital of the Chalukya (later Kalachuri) rulers. Basavanna rejected caste, Vedic ritualism and the authority of the Brahmins, and insisted that every devotee must wear the *ishtalinga* (a personal linga) on the body. Ramanuja (A) founded Vishishtadvaita; Madhva (C) founded Dvaita in Udupi; Kabir (D) was a north Indian nirguna sant, not a Lingayat founder.

**Trap:** Ramanuja and Madhva, like Basavanna, are 11th-13th century south Indian reformers, so students tend to mix up who did what. The Lingayat movement is exclusively associated with Basavanna and Kalyana, not with Srivaishnavism or Dvaita.
questions.wikilink: [[../../history/16 - Bhakti and Sufi Movements.md#Content|Bhakti and Sufi Movements — source chapter]]

questions.subject: history
questions.question: Which Sikh Guru established the Khalsa Panth in 1699 at Anandpur?
questions.explanation:
Guru Gobind Singh, the tenth Sikh Guru, established the Khalsa Panth at Anandpur Sahib in 1699 CE on the day of Baisakhi. He gave the Sikhs the five Ks (kesh, kangha, kara, kachera, kirpan) and the initiation rites of *amrit* and the surname "Singh" / "Kaur". Guru Nanak (A) was the founder of Sikhism. Guru Arjan (B) compiled the Adi Granth. Guru Hargobind (C) militarised the Sikh community after his father Arjan's martyrdom but did not found the Khalsa.

**Trap:** Several Gurus are associated with military or organisational reforms (Arjan built the Harmandir Sahib and Hargobind wore two swords, *miri-piri*), but only Gobind Singh actually instituted the Khalsa in 1699.
questions.wikilink: [[../../history/16 - Bhakti and Sufi Movements.md#Content|Bhakti and Sufi Movements — source chapter]]

questions.subject: history
questions.question: A student reads that a saint-poet rejected both Hindu ritualism and Islamic formalism, used local Hindi dialects, and his verses were collected in the *Bijaka*. The saint being described is:
questions.explanation:
The description fits Kabir (c. 1440-1518 CE). Kabir criticised empty ritualism from both Hindu and Muslim sides, preached a nirguna (formless) devotion expressed in popular Hindi dialects (Avadhi, Bhojpuri), and his verses were preserved by his disciple Bhago Das in the compilation known as the *Bijaka*. Guru Nanak (B), though he too preached a monotheistic path in Punjabi, is associated with the *Adi Granth* and the founding of Sikhism rather than the Bijaka. Chaitanya (C) was a Krishna-bhakti devotee in Bengal, not a nirguna critic of ritual. Mirabai (D) was a Krishna-bhakti poet-princess from Rajasthan.

**Trap:** Kabir and Guru Nanak both rejected ritual and used vernacular languages, so the giveaway here is the specific text mentioned — *Bijaka* belongs only to Kabir.
questions.wikilink: [[../../history/16 - Bhakti and Sufi Movements.md#Content|Bhakti and Sufi Movements — source chapter]]

questions.subject: history
questions.question: The Sufi shrine at Ajmer (Dargah Sharif) is associated with:
questions.explanation:
The famous Sufi shrine at Ajmer, known as the Dargah Sharif, is the mausoleum of Khwaja Moinuddin Chishti, the founder of the Chishti order in India, who came from Persia/Chisht in Afghanistan and settled at Ajmer in the late 12th century. Nizamuddin Auliya (A) is the Chishti saint of Delhi, buried at the Nizamuddin dargah. Salim Chishti (C) is the Chishti saint of Fatehpur Sikri, not Ajmer. Baba Farid / Fariduddin Ganjshakar (D) is the Chishti saint of the Punjab-Haryana border region (Pakpattan).

**Trap:** Many students confuse the Ajmer dargah with Fatehpur Sikri because Akbar visited both. Only Ajmer, however, houses Moinuddin Chishti; Salim Chishti is buried at Fatehpur Sikri.
questions.wikilink: [[../../history/16 - Bhakti and Sufi Movements.md#Content|Bhakti and Sufi Movements — source chapter]]

questions.subject: history
questions.question: Which of the following is INCORRECT about the Bhakti Movement?

options.text: It was led mostly by women and lower castes
It was exclusively a North Indian movement
It coexisted with, rather than immediately replaced, Sufism

questions.explanation:
Statement C is incorrect: the Bhakti Movement was emphatically pan-Indian, not exclusively North Indian. Major centres existed in Tamil Nadu (Alvars and Nayanars), Karnataka (Basavanna, the Lingayats), Bengal (Chaitanya), Maharashtra (the Warkari sant tradition of Dnyaneshwar and Tukaram) and Rajasthan (Mirabai), as well as in Hindi-speaking north India (Kabir, Raidas, Tulsidas). Statement A is correct: devotion to a personal God was stressed over Vedic ritual and priestly mediation. Statement B is broadly correct: many Bhakti leaders were women (Mirabai, Andal, Akka Mahadevi) and from non-Brahmin or low-caste backgrounds (Kabir, Raidas, Chokhamela). Statement D is correct: Bhakti and Sufi traditions existed side by side for centuries, often influencing each other and producing shared practices and even shared shrine-sites.

**Trap:** Many textbooks emphasise the Hindi heartland (Kabir, Tulsidas, Mirabai), which leads students to imagine Bhakti as a North Indian phenomenon. But the earliest and arguably most influential Bhakti movements are the Alvars and Nayanars of Tamil Nadu, predating the North Indian sant tradition by centuries.
questions.wikilink: [[../../history/16 - Bhakti and Sufi Movements.md#Content|Bhakti and Sufi Movements — source chapter]]

questions.subject: history
questions.question:
Match the following:

| Saint | Sect / Movement |
|---|---|
| 1. Mirabai | a. Vaishnava bhakti in Rajasthan |
| 2. Chaitanya Mahaprabhu | b. Krishna bhakti in Bengal |
| 3. Basavanna | c. Lingayat in Karnataka |
questions.explanation:
Mirabai (1) was a 16th-century Rajput princess-poet who devoted her life to Krishna, making her a classic Vaishnava bhakti figure of Rajasthan (a). Chaitanya Mahaprabhu (2), the 15th-16th-century Bengali saint, popularised ecstatic Krishna bhakti (the *kirtana* tradition) in Bengal (b). Basavanna (3) founded the Lingayat movement in 12th-century Karnataka (c). So the correct match is 1-a, 2-b, 3-c.

**Trap:** Chaitanya and Mirabai are both Krishna bhakti saints and are easily swapped because both are famous for devotional singing and *kirtana*. The decisive clue is geography: Mirabai — Rajasthan, Chaitanya — Bengal.
questions.wikilink: [[../../history/16 - Bhakti and Sufi Movements.md#Content|Bhakti and Sufi Movements — source chapter]]

questions.subject: history
questions.question: Who is the patron saint of the Chishti order in India?
questions.explanation:
The patron saint (and founder) of the Chishti order in India is **Khwaja Moinuddin Chishti** (d. c. 1236 CE), whose dargah at Ajmer is the order's central pilgrimage site. All the other Chishti luminaries mentioned (Salim Chishti at Fatehpur Sikri, Nizamuddin Auliya at Delhi, Baba Farid at Pakpattan) trace their spiritual lineage (*silsila*) back to Moinuddin Chishti. Farid was in fact a disciple of Nizamuddin Auliya, who was in turn a disciple of Baba Farid — illustrating the chain of authority originating with Moinuddin.

**Trap:** The most famous Chishti shrines in popular memory are those of Salim Chishti and Nizamuddin Auliya, so students may pick one of them. But "founder" and "patron saint" is unambiguously Moinuddin Chishti.
questions.wikilink: [[../../history/16 - Bhakti and Sufi Movements.md#Content|Bhakti and Sufi Movements — source chapter]]

questions.subject: history
questions.question:
Arrange in chronological order of birth:

1. Ramanuja (traditional dates 1017-1137 CE)
2. Kabir (c. 1440-1518 CE)
3. Chaitanya (1486-1534 CE)
4. Guru Nanak (1469-1539 CE)
questions.explanation:
The correct chronological sequence is: Ramanuja (1017 CE) — Kabir (c. 1440 CE) — Guru Nanak (1469 CE) — Chaitanya (1486 CE). So the order is 1, 2, 4, 3. Option B (1, 2, 3, 4) is wrong because it places Chaitanya before Guru Nanak, but Chaitanya was born about 17 years after Nanak. Option C is wrong because it puts Kabir before Ramanuja. Option D is wrong because it begins with Guru Nanak, who is the latest of the four.
